The Whittaker Cookbook is filled with short and self-contained recipes that try to answer one
question at a time. Every recipe is fully executable so you can copy the code and run it easily in
your own environment.

## Getting started

Start here if you are new to Whittaker. These recipes cover the core workflow: fitting a model,
picking the right response distribution, and reading the output.

## Smooth terms

The smooth term (its basis type, basis dimension, and interaction structure) is the main modeling
decision in a GAM. These recipes cover the most useful smooth types and how to configure them.

<div class="section-cards section-cards-list" style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr; gap: 1rem; margin-top: 0.5rem;">

<div style="font-size: 0.9rem; color: #6c757d; line-height: 1.45;">Understand the default smooth basis and when to use it.</div>
</a>
</div>

<div style="font-size: 0.9rem; color: #6c757d; line-height: 1.45;">Choose k large enough to avoid underfitting, then let REML handle the rest.</div>

</div>

## Response families

The response family determines the assumed distribution of your outcome and the link function that
connects it to the linear predictor. These recipes show how to handle counts, binary outcomes, and
proportions (the most common departures from a Gaussian response).

<div class="section-cards section-cards-list" style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr; gap: 1rem; margin-top: 0.5rem;">
<div style="border: 1px solid #dee2e6; border-radius: 0.5rem; overflow: hidden;">
<a href="model-count-data-with-poisson.qmd" style="display: block; padding: 1.25rem 1.5rem; color: inherit; text-decoration: none;">
<div style="font-size: 1.1rem; font-weight: 600; margin-bottom: 0.35rem; color: #0d6efd;">Model Count Data with Poisson</div>
<div style="font-size: 0.9rem; color: #6c757d; line-height: 1.45;">Fit a GAM when the response is a non-negative integer count, such as events per interval.</div>
</a>
</div>
<div style="border: 1px solid #dee2e6; border-radius: 0.5rem; overflow: hidden;">
<a href="model-binary-outcomes-with-binomial.qmd" style="display: block; padding: 1.25rem 1.5rem; color: inherit; text-decoration: none;">
<div style="font-size: 1.1rem; font-weight: 600; margin-bottom: 0.35rem; color: #0d6efd;">Model Binary Outcomes with Binomial</div>
<div style="font-size: 0.9rem; color: #6c757d; line-height: 1.45;">Fit a logistic GAM for 0/1 responses. Predictions come back as probabilities.</div>

</div>

<div style="border: 1px solid #dee2e6; border-radius: 0.5rem; overflow: hidden;">

</a>

<div style="border: 1px solid #dee2e6; border-radius: 0.5rem; overflow: hidden;">
<a href="estimate-a-survival-curve-with-cox-ph.qmd" style="display: block; padding: 1.25rem 1.5rem; color: inherit; text-decoration: none;">

## Prediction and inference

A fitted GAM is most useful when you can generate predictions at new inputs and attach uncertainty
estimates. These recipes cover point predictions, standard errors, and several flavors of confidence
interval.

<div class="section-cards section-cards-list" style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr; gap: 1rem; margin-top: 0.5rem;">
<div style="border: 1px solid #dee2e6; border-radius: 0.5rem; overflow: hidden;">

<div style="font-size: 1.1rem; font-weight: 600; margin-bottom: 0.35rem; color: #0d6efd;">Predict on New Data</div>
<div style="font-size: 0.9rem; color: #6c757d; line-height: 1.45;">Generate fitted values for any set of covariate values after fitting (grids, held-out rows, or hypothetical inputs).</div>
</a>
</div>

<a href="get-confidence-intervals.qmd" style="display: block; padding: 1.25rem 1.5rem; color: inherit; text-decoration: none;">
<div style="font-size: 1.1rem; font-weight: 600; margin-bottom: 0.35rem; color: #0d6efd;">Get Confidence Intervals</div>
<div style="font-size: 0.9rem; color: #6c757d; line-height: 1.45;">Add pointwise, simultaneous, or prediction-interval uncertainty bands to any set of predictions.</div>
</a>
</div>
<div style="border: 1px solid #dee2e6; border-radius: 0.5rem; overflow: hidden;">
<a href="get-simultaneous-confidence-bands.qmd" style="display: block; padding: 1.25rem 1.5rem; color: inherit; text-decoration: none;">
<div style="font-size: 1.1rem; font-weight: 600; margin-bottom: 0.35rem; color: #0d6efd;">Get Simultaneous Confidence Bands</div>
<div style="font-size: 0.9rem; color: #6c757d; line-height: 1.45;">Get bands that jointly cover the whole fitted curve at 95%, not just each point in isolation.</div>

<div style="border: 1px solid #dee2e6; border-radius: 0.5rem; overflow: hidden;">
<a href="get-prediction-intervals.qmd" style="display: block; padding: 1.25rem 1.5rem; color: inherit; text-decoration: none;">
<div style="font-size: 1.1rem; font-weight: 600; margin-bottom: 0.35rem; color: #0d6efd;">Get Prediction Intervals</div>

<div style="font-size: 1.1rem; font-weight: 600; margin-bottom: 0.35rem; color: #0d6efd;">Extract Term-Level Contributions</div>

## Diagnostics and model selection

Before trusting a model's predictions you should verify that it is well-specified. These recipes
walk through basis dimension checks, residual analysis, and how to choose a smoothness selection
criterion.

## Data input

Whittaker accepts Pandas DataFrames, Polars DataFrames, plain dicts, and NumPy arrays
interchangeably. This section shows how to work with data formats you may already have on hand.

<div class="section-cards section-cards-list" style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr; gap: 1rem; margin-top: 0.5rem;">
<div style="border: 1px solid #dee2e6; border-radius: 0.5rem; overflow: hidden;">

<div style="font-size: 1.1rem; font-weight: 600; margin-bottom: 0.35rem; color: #0d6efd;">Use a Polars DataFrame</div>
<div style="font-size: 0.9rem; color: #6c757d; line-height: 1.45;">Pass a Polars DataFrame directly to fit() without converting to NumPy or pandas first.</div>
</a>
</div>
